The Disiunction Paradigm
(Kubler & Proskouriakoff)
No continuity of meaning between
ancient and modern eras.
Ethnographic fieldwork is merely an
"autopsy" on a dead civilization.
The Classic Maya possessed no
concept of gods or rich mythology.
The Continuity Paradigm
(Coe & Taube)
Deep, unbroken continuity
across 2,000 years.
Living ethnographic practice is
the key to decoding ancient
artifacts.
Mesoamerica shares a rich,
unified cosmological framework.

The Tortilla Hypothesis
• Glaring lack of comales (wide,
shallow ceramic griddles) in the
archaeological record.
• Absence of tortillas in ancient
mural art
The Tamale Reality
• Abundant deep ceramic bowls discovered.
• Glyphs for feasting distinctly depict tamales.
• San Bartolo murals show rounded baskets
overflowing with tamales.
• Continuity of the no waah ritual tamale
preparation today.

Akan: The Iconography of Decay
The Ak'bal Sign: Marking his brow with
the symbol for deep darkness.
The Bone Hairpin: A human femur
violently thrust through his hair.
The Cimi Mark: The symbol of death
resting on his cheek.
The Fleshless Mandible: A skeletal jaw
indicating active rot and fermentation.
Alcohol (chicha) is fundamentally created through rotting and fermentation. Akan embodies
the liminal state where intoxication ('false death') provides visionary access to the ancestors.

Ritual Humor: The Sanctioned Subversion
The State
• Rigid, hierarchical
world of Classic
Maya elites.
• Monumental
architecture and
strict orthodoxy.
• Solemn royal
accession and
bloodletting.
THE PRESSURE VALVE:
By embodying wild,
inappropriate, and
overly-aged behavior,
clowns publicly mock
the established social
order and critique
community misdeeds-a
practice surviving in
contemporary Tzotzil
festivals today.
The Clowns
• Anthropomorphized
wild animals
(monkeys, opossums).
• Old men shaking
rattles, smoking, and
drinking.
• Engaging in enema
rituals on private
ceramics.

Decoding the Temple of Quetzalcoatl
Tlaloc (Rain God)
Shell Platelet Armor:
The mosaic surface
represents physical
combat helmets, not
deity skin.
Shell Goggles:
Intimidating military
eye-armor, not the
organic rings of the rain
god.
Feline Muzzle: A broad, predatory snout
completely distinct from Tlaloc's anthropomorphic face.
Conclusion: This is the Teotihuacan War Serpent.

The Pyrite Mirror: Artifact of Power
Military Armor
Worn on the lower back
to protect the kidnevs in
combat.
Solar Emblems
Worn as blinding,
reflective manifestations
of the sun's power.
The Face: Flawlessly cut,
fitted, and highly polished
iron pyrite tesserae.
The Backing: Heavy
slate or sandstone.
Visionary Portals
Shiny, dark surfaces used as
cave-like portals for divination.

The Unbroken Thread
600 BC (Olmec)
The infant maize god rests
on an earth turtle.
700 AD (Classic Maya)
The Tonsured Maize god
resurrects from the central
pit of the cosmic turtle
shell.
1984 AD (Contemporary)
Yukatek Maya prepare noh
waah tamales and warn of
feathered serpents taking
flight.
200 AD (Teotihuacan)
The War Serpent establishes
the iconography of central
Mexican military power.
1400 AD (Postclassic
Mayapan)
Katun wheels carved into
13-scute turtle altars.
Kubler's "disjunction" was an illusion. From the Olmec to the modern Tzotzil and
Yukatek, the underlying grammar of the cosmos-sustenance, time, decay, and
power-remains a living, continuous language.
